There is a time element and human component to this.

We are required to register TO vote, but we are not required to remove our name from prior registrations.   When someone moves, the resistors office receives a list.  A human being, who is likely over worked, and working with an antiquated system must manually move voters from active to inactive.

What incentive does the resistors office have to maintain 'accurate' voter rolls?  Yes, it is the law, but does the law specify what 'Accurate' really means?  When you look at the full scope of work associated with the resistors office where does maintenance of the voter rolls rank in terms of priority?  What decisions are made based on voter registration?  Is money tied to the number of registered voters?  Is their an incentive to REDUCE the number of registered voters?

A valid Photo ID mitigates this risk.  The name must match the name and address on record.  A provisional ballot is cast if not provided.  The impact of erroneous voter rolls is simply in the voter participation calculation.

That brings up another issue.  Is voter apathy real  or is it simply the voter rolls are in error?  Or, is it a combination of apathy and erroneous, inflated denominator?

The Darwinian view: from the simple to the more complex, as the old complex fails, the simple has the chance to develop into the new complexity.

In other words, our seeming fracturing, atomization, decadence, our foul seediness (Hamlet: "Fie on't! ah, fie! 'tis an unweeded garden, / That grows to seed; things rank and gross in nature / Possess it merely.") is also producing the seeds and mutations of the new, as an unweeded garden does — the new and improved of the future.

Many of our old ways, our beliefs and habits, deserve to be broken apart and replaced. Breaking up of various sorts can be hard, painful, full of anguish. But it also opens space, makes opportunities for what may eventually prove to be the better. The dying of the big dinosaurs brought about the flourishing of the little mammals, the opening of Pandora's box released new forces, out of chaos comes the new order.

comments.name: Norma
comments.body: A further thought prompted by the Jason Arday debacle at my alma mater, Cambridge University:  Last year, a small group of female undergraduates founded the Cambridge University Society of Women, in support of women's rights and the right to single-sex association.  In response, certain of their fellow students subjected these young women to personal threats, vitriolic online abuse, and a targeted petition demanding their outright ban. These brave women persisted, demonstrating great personal courage, and the CUSW continues to flourish.  In complete contrast, while these women students, exercising their legal and human rights, were left to navigate a hostile environment, the university hierarchy actively shielded Jason Arday from credible allegations of plagiarism and credential fabrication, dismissing any investigation as a vile smear campaign and enabling police action against the journalist who exposed him. This stark juxtaposition—where female students of high intelligence and impeccable integrity were abandoned to the vicious hostility of a fashionable ideology, while a male academic (whose ill-written, garbage-stuffed PhD thesis I have read with horror) was protected from serious misconduct charges—exposes a systemic rot that pervades this and other institutions and compromises their moral and academic integrity.

People who have neither money, privilege, glamour, or hunkiness, just hearts capable of being touched, devotion,  persistence and striving to improve themselves and their relationship, and make something beautiful of what they have and the person and family they have made their life with.

I am under no illusion that it would ever see the light of day, though Lord knows there is room for something less formulaic than a Hallmark romance movie -or greeting card.  

The best selling work of fiction in the English language is probably Jane Austin’s Pride and Prejudice, which was published when romances were equally formulaic, and even more well mannered.  Austin takes a verbal rapier and slices the lady’s dropped handkerchief in two before it hits the ground.  Lizzy is a girl on the cusp of adulthood who shares some of the values of the time, but is steadfast in her values and fearless rather than submissive.  Her confrontation with the imperious Lady Catherine de Bourgh is on the short list for greatest verbal duels in the English Language.

Romances these days aspire to that kind of success.  They may write spunky, sharp-tongued heroines.  But there is little risk of inspired writing or being challenged by Hallmark.

This story brings to mind two remarkable measures of humanity’s ability to ignore clear and present danger.

The New York Times was reporting on scientific concern about a warming planet as early as 1895 — 131 years ago. Today we aren't dealing with a theoretical possibility. As this story documents, businesses are spending real money coping with extreme heat, fires, drought, storms and power failures. The wolf is no longer somewhere over the hill. It is here, costing us money, disrupting our lives and increasingly threatening lives around the globe.

Which brings me to Aesop. Some 2,600 years ago, he gave us “The Boy Who Cried Wolf.” We teach it to children: Ignore warnings long enough and eventually the wolf arrives.

What boggles my mind is that after more than a century of scientific warnings and increasingly unmistakable evidence, powerful people in Washington and their supporters still deny, minimize or simply refuse to confront planetary warming.

At this point, “a day late and a dollar short” seems absurdly quaint. We are generations late, and the human toll is rising. The 2025 Lancet Countdown estimates that heat alone is now associated with about 546,000 deaths worldwide each year.

How many more warnings do we need before we finally believe the wolf is here?

The term Superintelligence (and AGI) is meaningless - there's no clear definition by which one could establish whether you have "it", or not.  The one thing that we can comfortably say about Superintelligence is that, if your rival gets it before you, you're at a fatal disadvantage.  And so companies and countries are pouring unfathomable sums into making sure they don't get behind, and in the process creating new concentrations of wealth and power for a limited few.  Meanwhile, The current Sub-Superintelligence that we have today is doing a great job disrupting the world in ways that already have profound impact, and as the AGI-ers predict, we ain't seen nothin yet.  The truth is, we don't need AI to be any more super than it already is to see where it's all going.  But because we presumably haven't reached the point where AI becomes "super", the world is living in a state of frantic anticipation, lulled by a shocked acceptance of the seemingly inevitable future into kicking the can down the road - just like the frog that swims happily in the pot as the water slowly boils. Ceuta has been a fortified city since at least the 2nd Crusade. Probably longer than that. It commands a prime position near the Strait of Gibraltar. This is a major part of why Morocco does spend time and effort working on maintaining the security of Ceuta. It brings them significant economic benefits.

But there's a constant pressure and every once in a while, they open the relief valve and allow a bit of a reminder that their cooperation is about the only thing helping Spain keep Ceuta secure. This was a perfect storm of misinformation and lack of political will on Morocco's side to stop this in the outset.

But the fact that these aren't political refugees but, in truth, economic migrants make this even more complicated. Morocco is a fairly restive and safe country, with an impressive for the continent economy. But it's close to Europe and the EU markets and it can easily see that relative wealth. That leaves many young Moroccans frustrated they spend their lives working for cents on the euro compared to peers who, in the case of Ceuta, aren't even a few miles away.

comments.name: Ottawa Wolfe

Just a bit of insight from social psychology here - avoid the fundamental attribution error - that is avoid assigning characteristics to an individual for circumstances that are completely beyond our control.

Just a comparative note here: Americans are far more likely than others to attribute behavior to an individual independent of circumstances. We assign a very high level of individual responsibility to life outcomes, which can have some positive aspects as well - it keeps us motivated and moving forward. But it also means we tend to be pretty harsh toward ourselves and others.

Consider the following fact: Since 2000, the number of people aged 25-34 who still live with their parents jumped from 12% to 22%, and it's even worse in NYC, from 22% to 32%. 

What are we to conclude from these statistics? That New Yorkers are even bigger losers than the general population and it is absolutely the worst place to date others?

No - obviously we are dealing with massive economic factors that are shaping how people live their lives, and we should avoid attributing the mere fact of living with parents, or being unemployed, to them being bad dating material. Now it could be a sign of something else - but you need to judge the circumstances and the individual. In Ireland, by the way, 40% of this demographic still live with their parents.

So try to set aside quick judgements and try to see the person in front of you. They may surprise you with their resilience!

The diagnosis may belong to the man, but the woman’s body becomes the battlefield.
When my husband was diagnosed with severe male-factor infertility, varicocele surgery failed. To attempt a pregnancy, the medical burden shifted largely to me: intensive hormone treatments to produce multiple eggs for ICSI, in which a single sperm was injected into an egg.

 It's very rewarding to feel you are making a difference, helping people understand issues like how proposed zoning and development affects them, the process of siting landfills and freeways, covering classrooms and school board meetings. 
This editor understands "names are news" and the importance of his readers knowing he's invested in them.

A community here took over one experienced journalist/editor's labor of love to create a community newspaper that would report the facts and has made it into a nonprofit. The music, words and staging all combined to draw me towards the magnificent life-sized horses in the first act (who wouldn't want to touch their glossy coats?) and recoil in horror, while still mesmerized, at the cost of riding them in the second act. It is probably not lost on anyone that "horse" is a synonym for heroin in the drug world - but no explanation is needed.  I have never experienced opera like this. It is now, it is real, it is tragedy as it exists today.  Congratulations to all for this creative masterpiece and for the courage to address this issue with such frank and unsettling honesty. Go see it wherever you can.

comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body:
My God, does this nonsense never end? How many opera lovers or opera-goers (not always exactly the same thing) really want to visit the local noise pit at $100 or more a throw to hear an opera about the opioid crisis? Really? No doubt Mr. Gelb's social conscience will dictate that it should be put on here, but maybe an attack of overriding financial intelligence will prevail. 

I'm sorry that Ms. Mazzoli and her librettist have lost relatives and/or friends due to the opioid crisis, but to use it as an excuse to write an opera on a decidedly unpalatable subject smacks almost of license. On the paternal side of my family, I've last a father, a grandfather, three aunts, an uncle and at least four cousins to cancer, yet I have never felt I should be writing a play or opera libretto on Galloping Cancer. It wouild certainly be a tragic one. But I might counter it by writing one of the maternal side of my family, where there is no cancer, but only a kind of  creeping idiocy. That might make a good comic opera. Perhaps I could combine them - a kind of Amfortas-meets-Dulcamara scenario. Yes, i really must get this onto the opera stage before I croak. Hey, everybody else is doing it and I want my chance at temporary immortality!

The impact of pain medicine addiction on society and families is horrendous and ethically wrong. 
Kudos to M Mazzoli and others for creating music to address this harsh and painful reality ! Mazzoli’s prior compositions have been performed by the Cincinnati symphony orchestra. Looking forward to hearing more of her musical voice!

comments.name: Alexander Bain
comments.body:
A Google Books search found an earlier instance of "Galloping Cure", in Cosmopolitan in late 1963, in the headline of a short piece on the then-trendy "d-lysergic acid diethylamide tartrate, a supposedly non-addictive drug". Now known as LSD.

Kudos to the librettist and composer for resurrecting this apt phrase. If tickets aren't already sold out I would like to travel to SF to experience the opera. Since the early 1960s our mortality rate due to illegal drugs has gone up by a factor of 10 and is now roughly the same as our mortality rate from alcohol, which has merely doubled. It is a sad reflection of our way of life that we do so little about this, other than performative but useless exercises like blowing up suspected drug boats. If opera can help turn this around even a little bit, it will be a better use of my hard-earned money than my tax dollars being wasted by the DEA.

comments.name: Walter Goodman
comments.body: The “no such thing as a free lunch” problem is daunting and insurmountable. Medicare beneficiaries have significant deductibles, premiums and co-insurance which is why half of them opt for Medicare Advantage and so many others buy supplemental plans. Eliminating the cost-sharing would cause an explosion of demand, which raises the other major problem with “Medicare for All” which is the inadequacy of Medicare provider rates. With a few exceptions, Medicare pays physicians and hospitals at rates that fall below the average cost of care (and the resulting cost shift is a significant factor in high commercial insurance premiums) but above the marginal cost. And, if you lose $1 on every unit, you can’t make it up by increasing volume. Impose Medicare payment rates for all services and the high fixed cost health care delivery system will implode. When queried about this, Bernie Sanders (who’s never met a payroll in his life) says, they’ll have to be “more efficient” but that’s delusional.

Does one just say, I’ll come back again and maybe the second or the third time will be the charm? Is every night there like playing the lottery? It’s an expensive place. Does the price fall when the quality does? These last two reviews—Marcel and Bistro Ha—make plain your take on dining in New York, a take that’s been there the whole time but not so clearly. We should look for and value small, scrappy (newyorkie), young, ambitious places with food that we might not have encountered before. We should avoid large, well-healed, older, places (ambitious or not), with food that we are probably familiar with.  In the first case, we should overlook flaws. In the second, we absolutely should not. As a program, it’s understandable. It may even be admirable. For a lot of potential diners (diners, not just readers) it’s an odd guide, especially with prices what they are. You love expensive tasting menus, but that’s not realistic for everyone. I, personally, wish you could find more “solid” and “dependable,” and “very good,” even if they’re less exciting. Something I can count on, not gamble on.

Marginalia comes from Latin ‘margo’ meaning ‘border, brink, or edge’, and -alia’ a plural suffix meaning ‘things relating to’ or ‘collection of.’

comments.name: Charles Kaufmann
comments.body: I had a similar experience in 2012 with my Longfellow Chorus and Orchestra performing unpublished works by Samuel Coleridge-Taylor (1875–1912). This was before the SC-T renaissance; none of my professional musicians had heard of him. I had programmed SC-T's major work, "Scenes From the Song of Hiawatha," to correspond with the centennial of his death. On June 5, 2012, I wanted to recreate the June 5, 1912, premiere of his Violin Concerto by Maud Powell at what is now the Yale Norfolk Festival. The concerto was too long. But I found the unpublished concert piece Powell played as an encore, "Keep Me From Sinking Down." The manuscript was in the Royal Conservatory of Music library. SC-T's handwriting in letters is almost unreadable. His music manuscript is clear and exacting. I transcribed parts for my orchestra. Almost exactly 100 years later, day and time, we performed the encore on the same stage in Norfolk where Maud Powell played it. The orchestra accompanying Powell was made up of NY Phil musicians, whose conductor had recently been Mahler. It was as if Maud Powell and SC-T were present with us. It was one of SC-T's last works. He died suddenly three months later at the age of 37. This was not the only SC-T manuscript I transcribed: the Violin Concerto, "Overture to Hiawatha," several of his arrangements of "24 Negro Melodies" for piano. I tell this story in my feature documentary, "Samuel Coleridge-Taylor and His Music in America, 1900–1912." https://youtu.be/HebDy-sLdCs

“But maybe because he did this on vacation, basically, he was more relaxed. So his handwriting is actually very calm and clear.”

This is probably because Mahler did not compose directly to full orchestral score. He composed a sketch of only a few vertical lines; and later, he orchestrated the sketch. (His sketches can be quite rough in appearance.) This is a common method for composers writing complex music for larger orchestras.

Projections for global wildfires indicate a massive shift toward larger, hotter, and more unpredictable blazes:

By 2050: Conservative models project a ~30% increase in extreme fire events globally. Given recent accelerated heating and compound droughts, these thresholds are arriving decades early. 

PyroCB events (firestorms generating their own lightning and localized weather) will transition from rare anomalies to standard operational hazards. 

Historically immune regions—such as the High Arctic, permafrost zones, and Scandinavian boreal forests—will routinely experience severe seasonal burning. 

By 2075: Models project a >50% increase in extraordinary fires, but real-world nonlinear dynamics (fuel drying, pest-killed forest collapse, and accelerated warming) suggest even higher severity. 

Boreal and tropical peatlands risk entering permanent burning-rebounding cycles, turning critical global carbon sinks into massive net carbon sources. 

Extreme pyroCB activity will regularly inject massive smoke and aerosol plumes directly into the stratosphere, altering local weather patterns and degrading regional air quality for months at a time.

With so little information, how can random visa cancellations be tracked or explained?

Every summer for many decades our elderly Australian friend came to NYC to visit his daughter, an American citizen, and then to go to Europe for the tennis, see some theater in London, before returning to NYC where we would all celebrate his birthday.

Last summer he came to NYC as usual, went to Europe as usual, but the day before his flight from London to NYC he was notified that his visa waiver was cancelled and he would be denied entry to the US. 
No explanation, no appeal.

He lost his London-NYC ticket and his NYC-Sydney ticket and had to buy a last minute London-Sydney ticket.
And we had to cancel his 94th birthday party. 
He's not coming this year for his 95th birthday, can't risk it. 

If you are issued a visa (on in the case of Australians, a visa waiver) but it can be cancelled at any time, even mid-trip, without explanation, who can travel in reliance on one?
